paragraphs: The Sages of blessed memory said: one who buys or makes new garments recites Shehecheyanu, because he is joyful in them, and so he blesses Hashem, may He be blessed, for having merited him this joy. And although strictly the law would be to recite the blessing at the time of the purchase or the making, the world has become accustomed to reciting it at the time one wears the garment. But some say that if one bought or made some new garment, then when he puts it on he recites the blessing 'malbish arumim' (Who clothes the naked), and on a belt, when he girds himself with it, he recites 'ozer Yisrael bigvurah' (Who girds Israel with strength), and on a hat, when he places it on his head, he recites 'oter Yisrael betif'arah' (Who crowns Israel with glory). And some disagree and hold that these blessings should not be recited, and because of the doubt regarding these blessings the world has not become accustomed to reciting them. In any case, it is good to wear them for the first time in the morning and to have them in mind, and to put them on immediately after the morning blessings without any distraction or interruption, and by this he fulfills his obligation according to all opinions. And if he is compelled to wear them at night, he should say the aforementioned blessings without Hashem's Name and Kingship, and should mentally intend the Name and Kingship in his heart.

clarification.explanation: One who buys or makes a new garment that gives him joy recites Shehecheyanu, as thanksgiving to Hashem for having merited him this joy. By strict law one should bless at the time of purchase or manufacture, but the custom is to bless at the time of wearing. Some say that when one wears a new garment he also blesses 'malbish arumim,' on a belt 'ozer Yisrael bigvurah,' and on a hat 'oter Yisrael betif'arah'; but some disagree, and because of the doubt the custom is not to recite these. Good advice: wear them for the first time in the morning immediately after the morning blessings without interruption and have them in mind, and thereby fulfill all opinions; and if one is compelled to wear them at night, he should say these blessings without Hashem's Name and Kingship and mentally intend the Name and Kingship in his heart.
takeaways: A new garment that brings joy - one blesses Shehecheyanu (the custom is to do so at the time of wearing).
To also fulfill 'malbish arumim' and the others, wear them for the first time in the morning right after the morning blessings.

paragraphs: Even if one bought a garment that another person had already worn, as long as he is joyful in it he blesses Shehecheyanu; and the same law applies if a garment was given to him as a gift - even though it is not new, he blesses over it, since he is joyful in it.

clarification.explanation: Even if one bought a garment that someone else had already worn, as long as he is joyful in it he blesses Shehecheyanu. And likewise, if he received a garment as a gift, even though it is not new, he blesses over it, since he is joyful in it.
takeaways: The measure is joy: even a used garment or a gift requires Shehecheyanu if it brings joy.

paragraphs: On a shirt, trousers, shoes, and socks one does not bless, even though he is joyful in them. But on a half-garment such as what is called in Arabic 'yalak' (a knitted winter vest) or what is called 'sadriyye' (a buttoned vest), if they are significant and he is joyful in them, he blesses.

clarification.explanation: On a shirt, trousers, shoes, and socks one does not bless Shehecheyanu even though he is joyful in them. But on a significant outer garment (such as a winter vest/sweater) that gives him joy, he does bless.
takeaways: Basic/undergarments - no Shehecheyanu.
A significant outer garment that brings joy - one blesses Shehecheyanu.

paragraphs: If he is wealthy and made a new garment that is not significant to him and he is not joyful in it, he does not bless, even though this garment, if it belonged to poor people, would be significant to them and they would be joyful in it. This is the rule: whoever is joyful blesses, but one who is not joyful does not bless; and every person knows within himself how he feels.

clarification.explanation: A wealthy man who made a new garment that is not significant in his eyes and he is not joyful in it does not bless, even though that same garment would be significant and joyful to a poor person. The rule is: whoever is joyful blesses, and whoever is not joyful does not bless; and every person knows within himself how he feels.
takeaways: The blessing depends on personal joy, which varies from person to person.

paragraphs: One who buys new vessels that give him joy blesses at the time he uses them, but the world has not become accustomed to this - see Mishb'tzot Zahav at the end of section 223 for the reason. And since the custom has become established, even though the reason is weak, he should not bless, because the blessing of Shehecheyanu depends on custom. Nevertheless, one who is God-fearing should use them for the first time on the night of the festival and bring them before him when he says Shehecheyanu at Kiddush and intend to discharge them thereby, or he should use them when he has a new fruit over which to bless Shehecheyanu and intend them as well. And if he cannot manage this and wishes to use them immediately, he should then bless without Hashem's Name and Kingship and mentally intend the Name and Kingship in his heart.

clarification.explanation: One who buys new vessels that give him joy should, by strict law, bless Shehecheyanu at the time of use, but the custom has not been to bless (and the blessing of Shehecheyanu depends on custom). A God-fearing person should use them for the first time on the night of the festival and bring them before him when he says Shehecheyanu at Kiddush and intend to discharge them thereby, or use them when he has a new fruit before him and intend them as well. And if he is compelled to use them immediately, he should bless without Hashem's Name and Kingship and mentally intend the Name and Kingship in his heart.
takeaways: New vessels - the custom is not to bless over them alone.
It is worthwhile to combine them with the Shehecheyanu of a festival or of a new fruit.

paragraphs: One who built a new house or bought a house built by others blesses Shehecheyanu; but now the custom is not to bless Shehecheyanu over the house, but rather to make a chanukat habayit (house dedication) feast to give thanks to Hashem for this lasting good, and there is support for this feast from the words of our Rabbis of blessed memory in the Midrash (Tanchuma, Bereshit 4), and therefore it is called a se'udat mitzvah (feast of a commandment). And the custom is that the master of the house wears a new garment during that feast and blesses Shehecheyanu over it, intending it also for the house.

clarification.explanation: One who builds a new house or buys a house that is already built should, by strict law, bless Shehecheyanu, but now the custom is not to bless Shehecheyanu over the house, but rather to make a 'chanukat habayit' feast to give thanks to Hashem for the good. The custom is that the master of the house wears a new garment during that feast and blesses Shehecheyanu over it, intending it also for the house.
takeaways: A new house - one makes a house-dedication feast.
One blesses Shehecheyanu by means of a new garment at the feast, intending it also for the house.

paragraphs: It is not specifically a whole house that was built - meaning the courtyard and all its rooms and upper stories - but even if he built, in a courtyard he already had, new rooms or upper stories in which he is joyful, he should do the same: buy a new garment to bless Shehecheyanu over, intending the new construction; but there is no need to make a dedication feast.

clarification.explanation: This is not specific to a whole house, but even if one added, to a courtyard he already owned, new rooms or upper stories in which he is joyful, he should buy a new garment and bless Shehecheyanu over it, intending the new construction; but for this there is no need to make a dedication feast.
takeaways: Even a significant addition of construction requires Shehecheyanu (by means of a garment), without a feast.

paragraphs: Although our Sages of blessed memory said that if one's wife gave birth to a male he blesses 'HaTov VeHaMeitiv,' the world has not become accustomed to reciting this blessing, and the custom has only been that the father blesses Shehecheyanu at the time of the circumcision. And if the father is not present and the relatives circumcised the child, one does not bless; however, some say that when the father comes afterward he should bless Shehecheyanu when he sees the infant, since he is then joyful at seeing him; and some disagree about this. Therefore, in a place where the custom is to bless, they should bless, and in a place where there is no known and clear custom about this, they should not bless, because we hold that in a case of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient; rather, he should endeavor to bless over a new garment or a new fruit at the time he sees the infant and intend it for this as well. And at the time that I taught this matter in public, my teacher the Rav of blessed memory was present, and he testified regarding the crown of his head, the great Rav, my teacher, my grandfather, our Rabbi Moshe Chaim of blessed sainted memory, that he saw a certain father who was in another city at the time of the circumcision, and who came afterward, and he told him to bless Shehecheyanu, as 'Erech Lechem' and the Halachot Ketanot and their like have written. And from this testimony we learn that the custom of our city from ancient times has been to bless - and therefore the Rav, my teacher's grandfather, of blessed memory, instructed that man to bless, even though he knew that there is a dispute about this matter.

clarification.explanation: Although the Sages said that one whose wife bore a son blesses 'HaTov VeHaMeitiv,' this has not been the custom; rather, the custom has been that the father blesses Shehecheyanu at the time of the circumcision. If the father is not present and relatives circumcised the child, one does not bless; and some say that when the father comes afterward and sees the infant with joy, he should bless Shehecheyanu. Because of the dispute: in a place where the custom is to bless, they should bless, and where there is no clear custom, they should not bless (a case of doubt regarding blessings is resolved leniently), but rather he should bless over a garment or new fruit at the time he sees the infant and intend it for this as well. And from this testimony the Ben Ish Chai learned that the custom of his city from ancient times has been to bless - and therefore a father who was not present at the circumcision blesses Shehecheyanu when he sees the infant.
takeaways: The birth of a son - the custom is that the father blesses Shehecheyanu at the circumcision.

A father who was not present blesses Shehecheyanu upon seeing the infant, since the custom of our city from ancient times has been to bless; and where there is no clear custom, he should bless over a garment or new fruit and intend it for this as well.

paragraphs: When one reaches sixty or seventy, it is proper to wear a new garment or take a new fruit and bless Shehecheyanu over it, intending it also for his years; and some make a feast when they reach seventy. And the custom here in our city, may it be protected, is that one who brings a new Torah scroll to the synagogue on Shabbat or on a festival makes a feast at night for friends and companions, and in the middle of the feast he puts on a new garment and blesses Shehecheyanu, intending it also for the Torah scroll. And at dawn they bring the Torah scroll to the synagogue with a great gathering of the community and songs and great joy, and whoever does more of this is praiseworthy.

clarification.explanation: Upon reaching sixty or seventy, it is proper to wear a new garment or take a new fruit and bless Shehecheyanu, intending it also for one's years; and some make a feast upon reaching seventy. The custom of Baghdad: one who brings a new Torah scroll to the synagogue makes a feast, wears a new garment during it, blesses Shehecheyanu, and intends it for the Torah scroll.
takeaways: Reaching sixty/seventy - one blesses Shehecheyanu (by means of a garment/fruit) intending it for one's years.

paragraphs: On a fruit that renews itself from year to year and has a fixed time for its growth, one blesses Shehecheyanu; but fruits that have no distinguishing feature between old and new, such as walnuts and almonds, called in Arabic 'gawz' (pecan) and 'lawz' (almond), and 'bunduk' (small nut) and 'fustuq' (pistachio, 'garden of Eden nut'), even though they renew from year to year and one knows regarding these that he is blessing over ones that are new that year - even so, he does not bless Shehecheyanu, since there is no distinguishing feature in their body between new and old.

clarification.explanation: On a fruit that renews from year to year and has a fixed time for its growth, one blesses Shehecheyanu. But fruits that have no distinguishing feature between old and new, such as walnuts and almonds of various kinds, even though they renew from year to year and even though one knows that these are from the new crop - one does not bless Shehecheyanu over them, because there is no distinguishing feature in their body between new and old.
takeaways: A seasonal fruit with a fixed growing time - Shehecheyanu.
Walnuts and almonds (no distinguishing feature between new and old) - no Shehecheyanu.

paragraphs: On a fruit called 'nomi' (a small citrus fruit, sour) and a fruit called 'burtuqal' (orange), by strict law one should bless Shehecheyanu, since they renew from year to year and are also distinguishable in their body between new and old ones. But the custom here in our city has been not to bless Shehecheyanu over them, and I have heard that in the Land of Israel, may it be rebuilt and established, they have also not become accustomed to blessing - and the blessing of Shehecheyanu depends on custom. However, regarding the etrog, the Rav Peri Ha'adamah testified that the custom in the holy city of Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt and established, is to bless Shehecheyanu over it, since they eat it on the second night of Rosh Hashanah in place of a new fruit. And here in our city, may it be protected, the etrog is sweet but not very plentiful, only a little, and our custom in our house is to eat an etrog before the festival of Sukkot and to bless Shehecheyanu over it; but the community of our congregation does not generally have it available to eat before Sukkot, and they only eat it on the fifteenth of Shevat when it is brought for sale, and even those who bought an etrog for the waving preserve it until the fifteenth of Shevat and eat it then; and these do not need to bless Shehecheyanu, because they already blessed Shehecheyanu on the first day of the festival of Sukkot upon taking the lulav, and thereby the etrog is also discharged from the Shehecheyanu of eating, as the later authorities of blessed memory have written, and so I have concluded in the holy book Makabtziel.

clarification.explanation: On certain citrus fruits (such as oranges), by strict law one should bless Shehecheyanu - since they renew from year to year and are distinguishable in their body between new and old - but in Baghdad the custom has been not to bless, and he has also heard that in the Land of Israel they have not become accustomed to blessing (and Shehecheyanu depends on custom). Regarding the etrog, he testified that in Jerusalem the custom is to bless Shehecheyanu when eating it on the second night of Rosh Hashanah as a new fruit; the custom of Rabbi Yosef Chaim's family is to eat an etrog before the festival of Sukkot and bless Shehecheyanu; and one who eats it after having taken it with the lulav does not need Shehecheyanu, since he was already discharged by the Shehecheyanu of the first day of the festival of Sukkot.
takeaways: Certain citrus fruits - the custom has been not to bless Shehecheyanu.
Etrog - customs vary; an etrog taken with the lulav and eaten afterward is exempt from Shehecheyanu.

paragraphs: On turnip, called in Arabic 'shalgham' (white turnip), and likewise on a vegetable called in Arabic 'lahana' (cabbage), and likewise on lettuce called in Arabic 'khass' (lettuce), one blesses Shehecheyanu, since they renew from year to year. And on long cucumbers called in Arabic 'tarouzi' (long thin cucumber) one blesses Shehecheyanu, and one should not say that they are included in the category of short cucumbers called 'khiyar' (common cucumber), because they differ in name, in appearance, and in taste. But on vegetables that are leeks and celery, and also what is called in Arabic 'ma'danus' (parsley), one does not bless, because they grow all year round and there is no fixed time for their renewal.

clarification.explanation: On turnip, cabbage, and lettuce one blesses Shehecheyanu, since they renew from year to year. Also on long cucumbers one blesses, and one should not say that they are included in short cucumbers, because they differ in name, appearance, and taste. But vegetables such as leeks, celery, and parsley - one does not bless, because they grow all year round and there is no fixed time for their renewal.
takeaways: Seasonal vegetables (turnip, cabbage, lettuce, long cucumber) - Shehecheyanu.
Vegetables that grow all year (celery, parsley) - no Shehecheyanu.

paragraphs: Here in our towns there are several kinds of dates, and there are two that differ from each other in appearance, taste, and name, and they are a kind called 'kastawi' (a bright small, juicy date) and a kind called 'bagban' (a yellow, fleshy date) which are black. Even so, if he blessed over the kind called 'kastawi,' he should not bless Shehecheyanu again over the kind called 'bagban,' because although each one has its own particular name, nevertheless, generally speaking, they are all called by the name 'dates.' However, a God-fearing person should bring before him at the time of the blessing of Shehecheyanu three kinds - what is called 'kastawi' and what is called 'bagban' and what is called 'zidi' (a common, dark date) - and bless Shehecheyanu to discharge them all, and so we are accustomed to do in our house from the days of our fathers and our fathers' fathers. And here in our towns there are sweet mulberries that come out in the month of Iyar, and after a month other mulberries come out that have a somewhat sour taste, and they are called in Arabic 'mulberries of Damascus,' and the custom is to bless Shehecheyanu over both this and that.

clarification.explanation: There are several kinds of dates that differ in appearance, taste, and name, but if one blessed Shehecheyanu over one kind, he does not bless again over another kind, because they are all generally called 'dates.' A God-fearing person brings before him at the time of the blessing three kinds in order to discharge them all. And likewise regarding two kinds of mulberries (sweet ones that come out in Iyar, and afterward sourish mulberries), the custom is to bless Shehecheyanu over this one and that one.
takeaways: Different kinds of the same fruit (dates) - one Shehecheyanu discharges all of them.
One who wishes to be meticulous brings several kinds together at the time of the blessing.

paragraphs: One who eats a fruit that has not finished ripening does not bless Shehecheyanu over it. Now if he then ate it again after it finished ripening, some say he should bless Shehecheyanu, and some say he does not bless. And if such a thing happens to a person, he should bring another new fruit and bless over it, discharging this one as well; or he should hear the blessing of Shehecheyanu from another person and both should have intent. Therefore one should be cautioned here in our city about this matter regarding dates that are eaten before they finish ripening, called in Arabic 'guzi' (unripe dates) or 'kalal tosh' (before ripening), and likewise one must caution people regarding apples. However, regarding the practice of cooking apples with a meat dish before they finish ripening, there is no concern regarding the blessing of Shehecheyanu, because these apples that are placed in the cooked dish have their taste greatly changed and their form is also somewhat changed; therefore the plain custom here in our city is to bless Shehecheyanu when eating them raw after they finish ripening.

clarification.explanation: One who eats a fruit that has not finished ripening does not bless Shehecheyanu over it; and if he ate it again after it finished ripening - some say he blesses and some say he does not bless. In such a case he should bring another new fruit and bless over it, discharging this one as well, or hear Shehecheyanu from another. Therefore one must be careful regarding dates and apples that are eaten before they finish ripening. But apples that are cooked in a meat dish before they finish ripening are of no concern regarding Shehecheyanu (their taste and form change greatly), and the custom is to bless Shehecheyanu when eating them raw after they have ripened.
takeaways: A fruit eaten unripe - whether the blessing applies once it later ripens is disputed; one should discharge it via another new fruit or by hearing the blessing.
Apples cooked in a dish before ripening - no concern regarding Shehecheyanu.

paragraphs: One who ate and forgot and did not bless Shehecheyanu - some say he should bless over what he eats afterward, and some say he should not bless since he has already eaten; and in a case of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient, so he should not bless, but rather he should hear the blessing of Shehecheyanu from others, or discharge this one by means of another new fruit; and if he cannot do so, he should bless without Hashem's Name and Kingship and mentally intend the Name and Kingship in his heart.

clarification.explanation: One who ate and forgot to bless Shehecheyanu - some say he should bless over what he eats afterward, and some say he should not bless since he has already eaten; and in a case of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient - he should not bless, but rather hear Shehecheyanu from others or discharge it via another new fruit; and if this is not possible, he should bless without Hashem's Name and Kingship and mentally intend the Name and Kingship in his heart.
takeaways: Forgetting to bless Shehecheyanu - one does not bless it afterward (a case of doubt); he should hear it from another or discharge it via an additional new fruit.

paragraphs: It is written in the Jerusalem Talmud, end of the tenth chapter of Yuchasin: Rabbi Chizkiyah said in the name of Rav, a person is destined to give a reckoning and accounting for everything his eyes saw and he did not eat. Rabbi Elazar was concerned about that teaching and would set aside small coins and eat from every single new thing once a year - see there. Therefore, even the poorest of Israel should endeavor to buy from every new fruit to eat from it, he and his household, and to bless Shehecheyanu to give thanks to Him.

clarification.explanation: It is brought in the Jerusalem Talmud that a person is destined to give a reckoning and accounting for everything his eyes saw and he did not eat, and Rabbi Elazar would save small coins and eat from every new thing once a year. Therefore even the poorest of Israel should endeavor to buy from every new fruit and eat from it, he and his household, and bless Shehecheyanu to give thanks to Hashem.
takeaways: It is fitting to eat from every new fruit once a year and bless Shehecheyanu - and even the poor should make the effort to do so.

paragraphs: A male becomes obligated in the commandments at thirteen years and one day. Therefore, on the first day of his fourteenth year, the father should take hold of his son's hand and say, 'Blessed is He who has exempted me from this one's punishment,' and mentally intend the Name and Kingship in his heart, and he should endeavor to make a feast for friends and companions and invite Torah scholars to it, and increase the feasting and joy according to the good hand of Hashem upon him, for from this feast there will be a great defense for Israel, in that the advocating angels will say before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the world, see how joyful Your children are over entering the yoke of Your commandments. And this feast is called a se'udat mitzvah, and the aforementioned blessing without Hashem's Name and Kingship - the father should say it during the feast, and those seated should bless the son that he merit Torah, fear of Heaven, and the fulfillment of the commandments, and the elders among those invited should place their hands on his head and bless him with the Priestly Blessing. And if the son knows how to expound words of Torah, he should expound something fitting for the occasion - how good; and if not, the father should expound; and if not, one of the Torah scholars among the invited guests should expound. And it is good that the son wear a new garment and bless Shehecheyanu, intending also his entering that day into the yoke of the commandments; and if he lacks the means, he should bless over a new fruit. And also the daughter, on the day she enters into obligation of the commandments - although the custom has not been to make a feast for her - nevertheless, there should be joy on that day and she should wear Shabbat garments, and if she has the means, she should wear a new garment and bless Shehecheyanu, intending also her entering into the yoke of the commandments. And some are accustomed to make each year the day of birth into a festive day, and it is a good sign, and so we are accustomed in our house.

And I have heard that there are places accustomed to make each year a feast on the day a person entered into the covenant of Abraham our father, and it is a lovely custom and very pleasing to me, but we have not been accustomed to this in our house; only I myself, servant that I am, have been accustomed to say each and every year, on the day I entered into the covenant of Abraham our father, this petition: Master of the world, it is revealed and known before You that on this day, which is the such-and-such day of such-and-such month, which was the eighth day from my birth, I entered into the covenant of Abraham our father, peace be upon him, in the first year that I was born, and Your servant my father fulfilled in me the commandment of circumcision and periah as You commanded us in Your holy Torah, and the third vessel of the true foundation, called the Holy of Holies, was revealed and its light went forth, and the grip of the external forces was nullified, and seventy-eight lights of kindness were joined with seventy-eight lights of might, and the lights of might were sweetened in the lights of kindness. I beseech You, Hashem, for the sake of Your great Name and for the sake of Your mercies and kindnesses, help me and assist me to keep the desire of the holy covenant which You sealed in our flesh, and save me from every sin and from every evil thought and blemished notion, and save me from every blemish of the covenant, whether in thought, in speech, or in deed, whether through the sense of sight, the sense of hearing, or the other senses, and in all of them may I be pure in the holiness of the covenant without any blemish or evil thought whatsoever, and grant me merit that I overcome the evil inclination, and let my thought be bound and attached to constant holiness, for in Your abundant mercy You chose us from among all the nations and raised us above every tongue, and set us apart from all their impurities and abominations, as is written in Your Torah (Leviticus 10:26), 'And I have set you apart from the peoples to be Mine.' We give thanks to You, Hashem our God and God of our fathers, for having brought us out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed us from the house of bondage, and for Your covenant which You sealed in our flesh, and for Your Torah which You taught us, and for the statutes of Your will which You made known to us, and for the life and sustenance with which You feed and provide for us. I beseech You, Hashem, create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew within me a steadfast spirit, and draw upon me holy, pure, worthy, and correct thoughts, and let me have a heart that rejoices in Your service always, and help me for the sake of the honor of Your Name from now and forever. Amen, so be it Your will.

clarification.explanation:
A male becomes obligated in the commandments at thirteen years and one day. On the first day of his fourteenth year, the father takes his son's hand and says, 'Blessed is He who has exempted me from this one's punishment,' mentally intending the Name and Kingship in his heart (without saying it aloud). It is proper that the father endeavor to make a feast for friends and Torah scholars, and increase joy at it greatly - for it is truly a se'udat mitzvah, since it constitutes a great defense for Israel, as the ministering angels say before the Holy One, blessed be He: 'See how joyful Your children are to enter the yoke of Your commandments.' Those present bless the son that he merit Torah, fear of Heaven, and fulfillment of the commandments; the elders among the guests place their hands on his head and bless him with the Priestly Blessing; and if the son can expound words of Torah, he should do so himself, and if not, the father, and if not, one of the Torah scholars among the guests. It is good for the son to wear a new garment and bless Shehecheyanu, intending also his entering into the yoke of the commandments, and if this is not possible, he blesses Shehecheyanu over a new fruit. Also the daughter, on the day she enters into obligation of the commandments - even though the custom has not been to make a feast for her - should nonetheless rejoice that day and wear Shabbat clothing, and if possible wear a new garment and bless Shehecheyanu, intending also her entering into the yoke of the commandments.
Some are accustomed to celebrate the birthday each year as a kind of personal festive day, and this is a good sign. The Ben Ish Chai adds that in other places there is another lovely custom entirely: to make each year a feast on the day a person entered the 'covenant of Abraham our father' - that is, the anniversary of his own circumcision. This custom was not practiced in his house, but he relates that he himself was accustomed to say each year, on the anniversary of his circumcision, a personal petition before Hashem built also on kabbalistic foundations: according to the Kabbalah, on the day of the circumcision itself the 'third vessel of the foundation,' called the 'Holy of Holies,' was revealed and its light went forth, thereby nullifying the grip of the external forces (the sitra achra), and the seventy-eight lights of kindness were joined with the seventy-eight lights of might, thus sweetening the lights of might within the lights of kindness. Against this background, in the petition he mentions the day of his circumcision, asks to preserve the holiness of the covenant of circumcision from any blemish (in thought, speech, and deed), to merit overcoming the evil inclination, and gives thanks to Hashem for having brought Israel out of Egypt and for the covenant, the Torah, and the statutes given to the people of Israel.
takeaways: At age thirteen years and one day, the father says 'Blessed is He who has exempted me from this one's punishment' and holds a se'udat mitzvah, including the guests' blessing and the Priestly Blessing for the son.
The daughter, too, should be made joyful on the day she enters obligation in the commandments and should bless Shehecheyanu, even if the custom has not been to make her a feast.

There is an additional custom to celebrate each year both the day of birth and the anniversary of the circumcision (the covenant of Abraham our father), and to say on that day a personal petition about preserving the holiness of the covenant.

According to the Kabbalah, the day of circumcision is connected to the revelation of the 'foundation' (Holy of Holies) and the joining of the lights of kindness and might - hence the root importance of preserving the holiness of the covenant.
